own_scenes.place: Nueva York (dormitorio de la NYU, Elizabeth Street)
own_scenes.desc: Rick Rubin, estudiante de veintiún años de la NYU que creía que «el rap era rock», fundó Def Jam en su dormitorio produciendo «It’s Yours» de T La Rock & Jazzy Jay; Aaron Fuchs le aconsejó buscar a Russell Simmons, un promotor con carisma, hijo de un activista de los derechos civiles, que veía el hip hop como la expresión de una comunidad. Juntos lo sacaron de los parques a la radio y a MTV con un acuerdo de distribución con CBS/Columbia y una nómina que definió la nueva escuela: LL Cool J, Beastie Boys, Slick Rick, Public Enemy, EPMD. Sin radio negra, Bill Stephney trabajaba las emisoras universitarias y la «radio de la calle» de los radiocasetes; la prensa punk de la Village Voice los adoraba. Lyor Cohen, promotor de Los Ángeles, llegó a Nueva York sin trabajo, fue road manager de Run-DMC y consiguió el primer contrato de patrocinio del hip hop con Adidas al hacer que el público del Madison Square Garden alzara sus zapatillas en «My Adidas». En la sede caótica de Elizabeth Street, Faith Newman puso orden en los derechos de autor. En 1988 Rubin se fue a Def American y Cohen presidió Def Jam; en 1990 la dirigían mujeres; en 1999 Simmons vendió su parte a Universal por cien millones y extendió la marca a Phat Farm y Def Comedy Jam. El libro recuerda las acusaciones de abusos contra Simmons.

refs.q: Rick believed that rap was rock. It was all rock to him.
refs.para: Rick is not a Black man. But he was a fan of rap music. As an aspiring record producer, he thought there was a gulf between the excitement of a rap on record versus the excitement of live rap. Rick’s whole idea was, Might there be a way for us to capture the excitement of live rap on a record? Rick believed that rap was rock. It was all rock to him.

refs.q: We’re going to pull the mainstream in our direction.
refs.para: Bill Adler (journalist, Def Jam publicist): Russell’s idea was, “We do not have to crossover. We’re going to pull the mainstream in our direction. We’re going to produce recordings that are full-strength rap, and we have enough faith in the intrinsic power of this music to communicate directly and effectively with listeners, that we’re just going to let it be.”

refs.q: This is teenage music. This is about rebellion.
refs.para: I worked with Russell Simmons because he managed some of our groups, and if you were involved in hip-hop, you knew Russell. He drew those comparisons to rock and roll, punk rock, heavy metal. Like he always said, “Don’t try to narrow-cast this form. This is teenage music. This is about rebellion.”

refs.q: I think that’s when you knew the power of hip-hop, the power of what the future of branding is going to look like.
refs.para: Faith Newman (Def Jam): Being in Madison Square Garden when they performed “My Adidas” and people took off their Adidas and raised them in the air, I think that’s when you knew the power of hip-hop, the power of what the future of branding is going to look like. That was a big turning point.
